families.stem: Solve for $x$: $\dfrac{{=a}}{x}={=b}$
solution: The variable $x$ is in the denominator, and division by $0$ is undefined, so there is a restriction: $x\neq 0$.
Multiply both sides of the equation by $x$ to clear the denominator: $\begin{aligned}\frac{{=a}}{x}&={=b}\\{=a}&={=b}x\end{aligned}$
Divide both sides by ${=b}$: $\begin{aligned}x&=\frac{{=a}}{{=b}}\\x&={=s}\end{aligned}$

Check the answer by substituting $x={=s}$ back into the original equation: $\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\frac{{=a}}{{=s}}\\&={=a // s}\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$ Both sides are equal, and ${=s}\neq 0$, so the restriction is respected and $x={=s}$ is the solution.
families.notes: Entry-point skill: the variable is alone in one denominator and the right-hand side is a whole number, so the only moves are state x != 0, multiply both sides by x, divide by the coefficient, and check by substitution. It is the simplest case of the book's ex4-1-15 (4/p = 16/24, page 78, which cross-multiplies) and its solution follows the four steps of worked example 2 (restriction, multiply, solve, check by substitution). Parameters: the answer s is drawn first (2 to 12) and the right-hand side b (2 to 9), so a = b*s is always exactly divisible and the answer is always a positive whole number (largest numerator 108). That gives 88 distinct (a, b) stems; the same numerator can recur but never with the same b and a different answer. The restriction is x != 0 for every instance and the answer is never 0, so no instance has an extraneous root. No distractors, so no misconception ids are attached; the catalogued misconception about the restriction seeming optional is addressed by the worked solution stating it in step 1 and re-checking it in step 4. The multiplies-only-the-fractions misconception cannot arise because there is no term without a denominator on the left. Standard and advanced tiers were not listed as gaps and are already covered by the book's own questions (ex4-1-25, ex4-1-27 standard; ex4-1-23, ex4-7-2g advanced), so no further families were written.

params.name: b
params.resample_while: lcm(a, b) == a or lcm(a, b) == b

families.stem: Solve for $x$: $\frac{x}{{=a}}+\frac{x}{{=b}}={=c}$
solution: The denominators are ${=a}$ and ${=b}$, so the common denominator is ${=d}$.
Multiply every term on both sides by ${=d}$: ${=d}\times\frac{x}{{=a}}+{=d}\times\frac{x}{{=b}}={=d}\times{=c}$
Cancel the denominators, because ${=d}\div{=a}={=m}$ and ${=d}\div{=b}={=n}$: ${=m}x+{=n}x={=t}$
Collect the like terms: ${=m+n}x={=t}$
Divide both sides by ${=m+n}$: $x=\frac{{=t}}{{=m+n}}={=r}$
Check by substituting $x={=r}$: $\frac{{=r}}{{=a}}+\frac{{=r}}{{=b}}={=r//a}+{=r//b}={=c}$, which equals the right-hand side.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill, modelled on book ex4-1-32 (x over two denominators, constant on the right). Denominators are drawn from 2..6 and never one dividing the other, so both multipliers m and n are at least 2 (no '1x' is ever printed) and the common denominator is a genuine lcm. The answer is built as k times the lcm and the right-hand side computed from it, so every instance has a whole-number answer (6 to 60). Hand-checked: a=2, b=3, k=1 gives x/2 + x/3 = 5, x = 6; a=4, b=6, k=2 gives x/4 + x/6 = 10, x = 24.

params.why: keep the answer non-zero and small enough for the book

families.stem: Solve for $x$: ${=b}-\frac{x-{=p}}{{=a}}={=c}$
solution: Multiply every term on both sides by the denominator ${=a}$: ${=a}\times{=b}-{=a}\times\frac{x-{=p}}{{=a}}={=a}\times{=c}$
The denominator cancels and the whole numerator stays in brackets: ${=a*b}-(x-{=p})={=w}$
Remove the brackets. The minus sign in front changes the sign of each term inside: ${=a*b}-x+{=p}={=w}$
Collect the numbers on the left: ${=s}-x={=w}$
Subtract ${=s}$ from both sides: $-x={=z}$
Multiply both sides by $-1$: $x={=r}$
Check by substituting $x={=r}$: $\frac{{=r}-{=p}}{{=a}}=\frac{{=r-p}}{{=a}}={=b-c}$, so the left-hand side is ${=b}-\left({=b-c}\right)={=c}$, which equals the right-hand side.
families.notes: Standard tier, generalises book ex4-1-28 (3 - (y-2)/4 = 4, answer -2). One denominator with a binomial numerator behind a minus sign; the twist is that the minus must change both signs in the bracket. The answer is r = a*b + p - a*c, so it can be negative as in the book; zero and |r| > 30 are rejected. Hand-checked: a=4, b=3, c=4, p=2 reproduces the book (x = -2); a=5, b=2, c=6, p=3 gives 2 - (x-3)/5 = 6, 10 - (x-3) = 30, 13 - x = 30, -x = 17, x = -17, and (-17-3)/5 = -4 so 2 - (-4) = 6.

params.name: b
params.resample_while: lcm(a, b) == a or lcm(a, b) == b

params.name: r
params.resample_while: r == 0 or r == q or u * r + p == 0 or h * r + j <= 0

families.stem: Solve for $x$: $\frac{{=u}x+{=p}}{{=a}}-\frac{x-{=q}}{{=b}}={=v}$
solution: The denominators are ${=a}$ and ${=b}$, so the common denominator is ${=d}$.
Multiply every term on both sides by ${=d}$: ${=d}\times\frac{{=u}x+{=p}}{{=a}}-{=d}\times\frac{x-{=q}}{{=b}}={=d}\times{=v}$
Cancel the denominators: ${=d}\div{=a}={=m}$, ${=d}\div{=b}={=n}$ and ${=d}\times{=v}={=w}$, so ${=m}({=u}x+{=p})-{=n}(x-{=q})={=w}$
Remove the brackets. The minus sign in front of the second bracket changes both signs inside it: ${=m*u}x+{=m*p}-{=n}x+{=n*q}={=w}$
Collect the like terms: ${=h}x+{=j}={=w}$
Subtract ${=j}$ from both sides: ${=h}x={=y}$
Divide both sides by ${=h}$: $x=\frac{{=y}}{{=h}}={=r}$

Check by substituting $x={=r}$ into the left-hand side: $\frac{{=u*r+p}}{{=a}}-\frac{{=r-q}}{{=b}}=\frac{{=m*(u*r+p)}}{{=d}}-\frac{{=n*(r-q)}}{{=d}}=\frac{{=w}}{{=d}}$, which equals the right-hand side ${=v}$.
families.notes: Advanced tier, generalises book ex4-1-24 ((x+2)/4 - (x-6)/3 = 1/2, answer 24): two binomial numerators, subtraction between them, and a fractional right-hand side. The book's own twist is the minus sign in front of the second bracket. Denominators come from {2,3,4,6} with neither dividing the other (so both multipliers m, n are at least 2); the first numerator carries x-coefficient u (2 or 3) and u is resampled so the collected coefficient h = u*m - n is at least 2 (no '1x' is ever printed). The answer r is drawn first and the right-hand side v = w/d computed from it, so v is a positive fraction or integer and every instance has a whole-number answer; r is kept away from 0, from q and from a zero first numerator. Hand-checked: a=4, b=3, u=2, p=1, q=2, r=5 gives (2x+1)/4 - (x-2)/3 = 7/4, 3(2x+1) - 4(x-2) = 21, 2x + 11 = 21, x = 5; a=3, b=2, u=3, p=4, q=5, r=-2 gives (3x+4)/3 - (x-5)/2 = 17/6, 2(3x+4) - 3(x-5) = 17, 3x + 23 = 17, 3x = -6, x = -2.

records.notes: Three numeric families, one per tier, each modelled on a book question of this objective (ex4-1-32, ex4-1-28, ex4-1-24, all page 78) and following the book's method: multiply by the common denominator, expand, collect, divide, check by substitution. The misconception list for this objective is empty and no family is mcq, so no distractors or proposed misconceptions are declared. No engine was run, so every parameter table, constraint and worked step was hand-checked on sample instances (recorded in each family's notes). Slugs differ in their first six letters (sum-of, minus-, binomi).

params.why: a zero constant term would drop a term from the answer, and the entry-level question should show all three terms of ax^2 + bx + c

families.stem: Write $(x+{=p})(x+{=q})={=k}$ in standard form $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$.
solution: Expand the brackets on the left-hand side by multiplying each term in the first bracket by each term in the second: $(x+{=p})(x+{=q}) = x^{2}+{=q}x+{=p}x+{=pq}$.
Add the like terms ${=q}x+{=p}x={=b}x$, so the equation becomes $x^{2}+{=b}x+{=pq}={=k}$.
Standard form has $0$ on the right-hand side, so subtract ${=k}$ from both sides: $x^{2}+{=b}x+{=pq}-{=k}=0$.
Work out the constant term: ${=pq}-{=k}={=c}$. The equation in standard form is $x^{2} + {=b}x {=cs} {=cm} = 0$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Multiplies only the first and last terms of the two brackets
proposed_misconceptions.description: Expands (x + p)(x + q) as x^2 + pq, so the middle term (p + q)x never appears in the standard form.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Moves a term across the equals sign without changing its sign
proposed_misconceptions.description: Writes x^2 + (p + q)x + pq + k = 0 instead of subtracting k, so the constant term is pq + k rather than pq - k.

families.notes: Entry point of the skill: a monic product (leading coefficient 1) equal to a positive constant, so the only moves are expand, collect the two x terms, and subtract the constant. It is the book's ex4-2-1 method at its smallest. The answer is unique: it is the left-hand side minus the right-hand side with a = 1, so nothing can be rescaled or sign-flipped. p and q are 2..7 so no coefficient of 1 has to be hidden; c = pq - k is never 0 and may be negative (the sign of the constant is the one place an instance can go wrong). The variable is x in every instance (the book uses r and d). Checked by simulation: 600 draws, all steps and the marker answer agree with an independent expansion.

params.why: at least one of the x term and the constant must survive, otherwise the answer is just a multiple of x^2
no common factor in the three coefficients, so the standard form is the only one and nobody needs to divide through

params.name: kbs
params.let: '' if kb == 0 else ('+' if kb > 0 else '-')

params.name: kbt
params.let: '' if kb == 0 or abs(kb) == 1 else str(abs(kb))

params.name: kcs
params.let: '' if kc == 0 else ('+' if kc > 0 else '-')

params.name: zn
params.let: '' if kb != 0 and kc != 0 else ' A term whose coefficient is zero is simply left out.'

families.stem: Write $({=at}x {=bs} {=bm})({=c}x {=ds} {=dm}) = {=et}x^{2} {=fs} {=ft}x {=gs} {=gm}$ in standard form $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$, with every term on the left-hand side.
solution: Expand the brackets on the left-hand side by multiplying each term in the first bracket by each term in the second: $({=at}x {=bs} {=bm})({=c}x {=ds} {=dm}) = {=ac}x^{2} {=ads} {=adt}x {=bcs} {=bct}x {=bds} {=bdm}$.
Write the equation with the expanded left-hand side: ${=ac}x^{2} {=ads} {=adt}x {=bcs} {=bct}x {=bds} {=bdm} = {=et}x^{2} {=fs} {=ft}x {=gs} {=gm}$.

Standard form has $0$ on the right-hand side, so subtract every term of the right-hand side from both sides. Each one changes sign as it crosses the equals sign: ${=ac}x^{2} {=ads} {=adt}x {=bcs} {=bct}x {=bds} {=bdm} - {=et}x^{2} {=fns} {=ft}x {=gns} {=gm} = 0$.
Collect the $x^{2}$ terms: ${=ac}x^{2} - {=et}x^{2} = {=kat}x^{2}$.
Collect the $x$ terms. Their coefficients add up to $({=ad}) + ({=bc}) - ({=f}) = {=kb}$.
Collect the constants: $({=bd}) - ({=g}) = {=kc}$.
Put the three results together. The equation in standard form is ${=kat}x^{2} {=kbs} {=kbt}{=kbx} {=kcs} {=kcm} = 0$.{=zn}

proposed_misconceptions.label: Changes the sign of only the first term when moving several terms
proposed_misconceptions.description: Moving the right-hand side x^2 + fx + g across the equals sign, subtracts the x^2 term but adds fx and g, so the x coefficient and the constant come out wrong.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Leaves the x^2 term on the right-hand side out of the collection
proposed_misconceptions.description: Treats the x^2 term on the right as something that stays there, so the leading coefficient is the product of the two x coefficients (ac) instead of ac minus the right-hand coefficient.

families.notes: Advanced tier: a product on the left and a quadratic trinomial on the right, so the book's expand-and-subtract method (ex4-2-1) needs three sign changes and three collections, and the x^2 terms do not stay as they were. Constraints: a in 1..3 and c in 2..3 so a*c >= 2 and e is drawn from 1..a*c-1, hence the leading coefficient ka = a*c - e is at least 1 (no negative a, no degenerate linear equation). The coefficients of the answer have gcd 1, so the standard form is unique and a blind solver has no reason to divide through; the stem fixes the side (all terms on the left). About one instance in thirteen has a zero coefficient (the x term or the constant cancels), which the book itself uses in ex4-2-1a; the solution then says a zero term is left out, and the marker answer carries it as + 0*x or + 0, which the engine should read as the same equation. b, d, f, g are never 0 so every factor and every right-hand term is present as printed. Checked by simulation: 600 draws, 600 distinct stems, every solution step and the marker answer agree with an independent expansion, and no draw needed more than 3 attempts.

records.notes: Both listed gaps (basic, advanced) are filled; the standard tier is the book's own exercise (monic-or-not product equal to a constant) and was not requested. The catalogue of misconceptions for this objective is empty, so no mcq was written; both families are expression type with an equation marker, and each declares two proposed misconceptions for the reviewer (none is attached to a distractor). I could not run the real engine (only the two packet files may be opened), so I checked the families with my own Python re-implementation of the param, let, require and template rules: every rendered step, the final line and the marker answer matched an independent polynomial expansion over 600 draws per family. Engine assumptions worth a glance when it first runs: string literals and str() inside let params (used to print signs and to hide a coefficient of 1 without string concatenation), empty-string holes rendering as nothing, and the equation marker reading '+ 0*x' as the same equation as one with the term omitted.

params.why: keeps the constant on the right-hand side as small as the book's own (18), so every instance factorises by inspection

families.stem: Solve for $x$ (note the restriction that applies): $x+{=m}=\frac{{=n}}{x}$
solution: The variable appears in a denominator, so $x\neq0$.
Multiply every term by $x$ to clear the fraction: $x^2+{=m}x={=n}$.
Move everything to the left so that the right-hand side is zero: $x^2+{=m}x-{=n}=0$.
Factorise the trinomial. Two numbers with product $-{=n}$ and sum ${=m}$ are $-{=p}$ and ${=q}$, so $(x-{=p})(x+{=q})=0$.
A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero, so $x={=p}$ or $x=-{=q}$.
Neither value is $0$, so both respect the restriction. Check $x={=p}$: $x+{=m}={=q}$ and $\frac{{=n}}{{=p}}={=q}$. Check $x=-{=q}$: $-{=q}+{=m}=-{=p}$ and $\frac{{=n}}{-{=q}}=-{=p}$.
Therefore $x={=p}$ or $x=-{=q}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: one fraction whose only denominator is the bare variable, a monic trinomial after multiplying through by x, and integer roots. Modelled on book exercise 4.2 Q3(c) (x + 2 = 18/x - 1, p. 81) with the constant folded into one term so the first step is only 'multiply by x'. Construction: roots are p > 0 and -q where q = p + m, so the equation x + m = pq/x always has one positive and one negative root, both non-zero. m starts at 2 so the expanded line never prints '1x'. 28 distinct (p, m) pairs survive the n <= 60 cap, enough for ten distinct stems. By design the restriction x != 0 never removes a root at this tier (both roots are non-zero), so the catalogued misconception mc:g10m4s3-1-3:keeps-a-root-the-restriction-forbids cannot be exercised here; that trap belongs to a family with a rational expression like book Q 4-7-12k, which is not a gap I was asked to fill. The answer is a values-marker with two values; the stem does not say how many solutions there are. All 28 instances were checked offline: both roots satisfy the original equation and x^2+mx-n equals (x-p)(x+q).

records.notes: Only the basic tier was listed as a gap, so one family is returned. Standard and advanced were not requested; the nine book questions already sit at standard, and the extraneous-root trap (misconception keeps-a-root-the-restriction-forbids) is left for a standard-tier family on a rational expression equal to a constant, modelled on book Q 4-7-12k. The family answer uses the values marker with plain maths [p, -q]; no mcq was used because no diagnosable distractor exists at this entry tier.

params.why: keeps every number small enough to work with by hand

families.stem: Solve for $x$ and $y$: $y = {=a}x + {=b}$ and $x + y = {=total}$.
solution: The first equation already gives $y$ in terms of $x$: $y = {=a}x + {=b}$.
Substitute this expression for $y$ into the second equation: $x + ({=a}x + {=b}) = {=total}$.
Collect the like terms: ${=a + 1}x + {=b} = {=total}$.
Subtract ${=b}$ from both sides: ${=a + 1}x = {=total - b}$.
Divide both sides by ${=a + 1}$: $x = {=xv}$.
Substitute $x = {=xv}$ back into the first equation to find $y$: $y = {=a}({=xv}) + {=b} = {=yv}$.
Therefore $x = {=xv}$ and $y = {=yv}$.
families.notes: Basic entry point of the skill. One equation already has y as its subject (y = ax + b, a in 2..4 so there is never a '1x'), the other is the simplest possible x + y = total, so the learner meets exactly the book's steps (ex4-3-4d, and ex4-7-6b/ex4-3-4c for the shape of the second equation): write y in terms of x, substitute, solve for x, substitute back for y. All coefficients and constants shown in the stem and the solution are positive and both solutions are positive whole numbers (x in 1..6, y = a*x + b <= 30), so every template sign is literal and no instance involves negative arithmetic, fractions or rearranging. Variation: 3 values of a x 9 of b x 6 of x gives well over 100 distinct stems. Answer is the ordered pair x then y, in the book's 'values' marker form. No mcq, so no misconception ids are used: none are catalogued for this objective. Standard and advanced tiers were not listed as gaps (the book's own exercises are standard), so no families were written for them.

records.notes: One basic family written: y = ax + b with x + y = total, all-positive whole-number solutions, following the book's substitute / solve for x / substitute back sequence. Only the listed basic gap was filled. The misconception catalogue for this objective is empty and no mcq was written, so no misconception ids were used or proposed. I did not run the family through the engine because I was limited to the two packet files, but the arithmetic was checked by hand: a=3, b=5, x=4 gives y=17 and total=21, and 4x+5=21 gives x=4, as the solution steps state.

params.why: keep both right-hand sides non-zero so neither equation looks degenerate

families.stem: Use elimination to solve for $x$ and $y$ : ${=p}x+{=q}y={=k1}$ and ${=r}x-{=q}y={=k2}$
solution: The coefficients of $y$ are ${=q}$ and $-{=q}$. They are opposites, so adding the two equations eliminates $y$.
Add the equations, left side to left side and right side to right side:
$\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{cccc}&{=p}x+{=q}y&=&{=k1}\\ +&({=r}x-{=q}y&=&{=k2})\\ \hline&{=tot}x&=&{=rhs}\end{array}\end{aligned}$
Solve for $x$ :
$\begin{aligned} {=tot}x&= {=rhs}\\ x&=\frac{{=rhs}}{{=tot}}\\ &= {=x}\end{aligned}$
Substitute $x={=x}$ into the first equation and solve for $y$ :
Therefore $x={=x}$ and $y={=y}$ .
families.notes: Entry point, modelled on book ex4-7-6a. The y-coefficients are already opposite (+q and -q) so one addition eliminates y; no multiplying is needed. Sign pattern is fixed in the template (+ in the first equation, - in the second), so all coefficients in the holes are positive and 2 or more (no printed '1x'). r != p keeps adding as the only direct route (if the x-coefficients were equal, subtracting would also work). x and y are non-zero integers in [-6, 6], so answers are whole numbers and may be negative; the determinant -q(p+r) is never zero, so the solution is unique. I checked all about 33,000 admissible parameter sets: x*(p+r) equals the added right-hand sides and q*y equals k1 - p*x in every one. Right-hand sides may be negative, as in the book question.

params.why: keep both right-hand sides non-zero so neither equation looks degenerate

families.stem: Use elimination to solve for $x$ and $y$ : ${=a}x+{=b}y={=k1}$ and ${=c}x-{=d}y={=k2}$
solution: No variable has equal or opposite coefficients yet. The coefficients of $y$ are ${=b}$ and ${=d}$, which share no common factor, so we multiply the first equation by ${=d}$ and the second equation by ${=b}$. Both equations then contain a $y$-term of size ${=bd}y$, one positive and one negative.
Multiply the first equation by ${=d}$ :
$\begin{aligned} {=d}({=a}x+{=b}y)&= {=d}({=k1})\\ {=ad}x+{=bd}y&= {=dk1}\end{aligned}$
Multiply the second equation by ${=b}$ :
$\begin{aligned} {=b}({=c}x-{=d}y)&= {=b}({=k2})\\ {=bc}x-{=bd}y&= {=bk2}\end{aligned}$
The $y$-terms are now ${=bd}y$ and $-{=bd}y$, so adding the two new equations eliminates $y$ :
$\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{cccc}&{=ad}x+{=bd}y&=&{=dk1}\\ +&({=bc}x-{=bd}y&=&{=bk2})\\ \hline&{=tot}x&=&{=rhs}\end{array}\end{aligned}$
Solve for $x$ :
$\begin{aligned} {=tot}x&= {=rhs}\\ x&=\frac{{=rhs}}{{=tot}}\\ &= {=x}\end{aligned}$
Substitute $x={=x}$ into the first equation and solve for $y$ :
Therefore $x={=x}$ and $y={=y}$ .
families.notes: Advanced, modelled on book ex4-3-4e (5x-4y=69 and 2x+3y=23), whose twist is that BOTH equations must be multiplied before they can be added: the y-coefficients b and d are chosen coprime and both at least 2, so neither divides the other and the lowest common multiple is b*d. Multiplying the first equation by d and the second by b gives +b*d*y and -b*d*y, and the equations are added (the book's ex4-3-4g/ex4-7-6a use the same layout). The book's own worked solution to ex4-3-4e uses substitution; the elimination method shown here is the one this objective teaches and is the same method as the book's solution to ex4-3-4g (multiply, then add/subtract, solve, substitute back). Sign pattern is fixed in the template (+b y in the first equation, -d y in the second), so every hole coefficient is positive and at least 2. a != c, so the x-coefficients are never equal. x and y are non-zero integers in [-5, 5], so the answers are whole numbers (possibly negative); the determinant -(a*d + b*c) is never zero, so the solution is unique. I checked all about 18,000 admissible parameter sets: (a*d+b*c)*x equals the added right-hand sides d*k1 + b*k2 and b*y equals k1 - a*x in every one; the largest intermediate number is 250.

records.notes: Two families, one per listed gap (basic and advanced), no standard family since only the gaps were requested. Answers are whole numbers by design, so every marker answer is a plain list [x, y] and none depends on how a fraction hole renders. No mcq: every distractor-style error here is the single catalogued mc:g10m4s4-1-2:subtract-only-some-signs, which belongs to subtraction, and both of my families use addition. Slugs differ in their first six characters (add-op vs scale-). I could not run the family engine in this session, so the template syntax is unvalidated by the engine. I put a space after every LaTeX row break and after \begin{aligned} before a hole, and kept all holes to bare names or simple products defined as let params. The arithmetic identities behind every worked step were checked by brute force over all admissible parameter sets. I did not write a fractions or reciprocal family (book ex4-3-4h and ex4-3-4k): clearing denominators first needs integer right-hand sides, which forces answers to be multiples of the denominators, and the reciprocal case has fractional answers that cannot be written as a plain marker answer without relying on how a fraction hole renders.

families.context: A rectangle whose length is a given number of centimetres more than its breadth has a given area in square centimetres. The question asks for the breadth. The quadratic that results has one positive and one negative solution, and only the positive one can be a breadth.

params.require: p > q and area == p * q and p - q == k
params.why: the two factors of the quadratic are x + p and x - q, with p - q = k and p * q = area, so every instance factorises cleanly over the integers

families.stem: The length of a rectangle is ${=k}$ cm more than its breadth. The area of the rectangle is ${=area}$ $\text{cm}^2$. Find the breadth of the rectangle, in cm.
solution: Let the breadth be $x$ cm. The length is ${=k}$ cm more than the breadth, so the length is $(x+{=k})$ cm.
The area of a rectangle is length $\times$ breadth, so $x(x+{=k})={=area}$.
Multiply out and move every term to the left-hand side: $x^2+{=k}x={=area}$, so $x^2+{=k}x-{=area}=0$.
Factorise. We need two numbers whose product is $-{=area}$ and whose sum is ${=k}$. These numbers are ${=p}$ and $-{=q}$, so $(x+{=p})(x-{=q})=0$.
Solve each factor: $x=-{=p}$ or $x={=q}$.
A breadth cannot be negative, so we reject $x=-{=p}$. The breadth is ${=q}$ cm.
Check: the length is ${=q}+{=k}={=p}$ cm, and ${=q}\times{=p}={=area}$ $\text{cm}^2$, as given.
families.notes: Basic-tier entry point of the skill: one unknown, one condition (the length exceeds the breadth by k), and one decision (the negative root cannot be a breadth). Modelled on book exercise 4.4 question 9 (rectangle, area given, 'breadth must be positive'), but with the length k more than the breadth instead of twice the breadth, so the equation is a trinomial that needs factorising rather than a difference of squares. The setup is x(x + k) = area, which becomes x^2 + k x - area = 0 and factorises as (x + p)(x - q) with p = q + k and area = p*q. The roots are q and -p, so the answer is always the single positive whole number q. The question asks for the breadth only, so the numeric answer is one value that a blind solver can state without a unit; the stem says 'in cm'. k starts at 2 so the middle term is never written with a coefficient of 1; q runs 2 to 10 and k runs 2 to 8, giving 63 distinct (k, area) stems with area at most 180. The Rand and other contexts are not used here. No mcq is offered, so the two catalogued misconceptions are not attached to distractors; the solution still states the rejection of the negative root explicitly, which addresses 'keeps a solution the problem rules out'. The 'throws away a negative solution without checking' error needs a problem with no sign condition, which belongs to the standard tier (book question 4.4 question 10: a number, answer 7 or -3).

records.notes: One basic-tier family written for the only listed gap (basic). Standard and advanced tiers were not requested. The family is a numeric rectangle problem with a fixed context. Its parent is book question ex4-4-9 on page 93. No distractors exist, so no misconception ids are attached.

params.why: keeps s a whole number: the term a t^2 / 2 must be whole

families.stem: Solve for $a$ in $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ if $s={=s}$, $u={=u}$ and $t={=t}$.
solution: Ask what $a$ is joined to. In $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ the term with $a$ is added to $ut$, so subtract $ut$ from both sides: $s-ut=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$.
Now $a$ is multiplied by $\frac{1}{2}$ and by $t^{2}$. Multiply both sides by $2$ to clear the fraction: $2(s-ut)=at^{2}$.
Divide both sides by $t^{2}$ (here $t\ne0$): $a=\frac{2(s-ut)}{t^{2}}$.
families.notes: Advanced: combines the book's ex4-5-2 rearrangement (three opposite operations: subtract ut, multiply by 2, divide by t^2, with the book's note t != 0) with the book's ex4-5-18 twist of substituting given values. The instance values are built backwards from a, t and u so s is always a whole number and the answer a is always a whole number between 2 and 9; s - ut is always positive. No decimals or rounding. Typical errors a reviewer may see in wrong answers: dividing ut-term-less s by t^2 without subtracting ut, multiplying by 1/2 instead of 2, or dividing by t instead of t^2. No misconceptions were catalogued for this objective, so none are referenced.

params.why: avoids trivial instances where h is 1 or equals E

families.stem: Solve for $\lambda$ in $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ if $E={=en}$, $h={=h}$ and $c={=c}$.
solution: Ask what $\lambda$ is joined to. In $E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$ the unknown $\lambda$ is in the denominator: $hc$ is divided by $\lambda$. The opposite of dividing by $\lambda$ is multiplying by $\lambda$, so multiply both sides by $\lambda$: $E\lambda=hc$.
Now $\lambda$ is multiplied by $E$, so divide both sides by $E$ (here $E\ne0$): $\lambda=\frac{hc}{E}$.
Substitute $h={=h}$, $c={=c}$ and $E={=en}$: $\lambda=\frac{{=h}({=c})}{{=en}}$.
Calculate: $\lambda=\frac{{=h*c}}{{=en}}={=lam}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the book's ex4-5-6 makes h the subject of E = hc/lambda (unknown in the numerator, one multiplication and one division). Here the unknown is lambda, in the denominator, which is the harder case: the first step must be multiplying both sides by lambda, as the book's own solution to ex4-5-6 does, then dividing by E. Substituting given values is the book's ex4-5-18 twist. Values are built backwards from lambda, E and c so h is a whole number and the answer lambda is always a whole number between 2 and 9; no decimals or rounding. A common wrong answer a reviewer may see is E/(hc) or hE/c (treating lambda as if it were in the numerator). No misconceptions were catalogued for this objective, so none are referenced. This is a lighter advanced item than accel-values; it is kept because it tests a distinct case (subject in the denominator) that the objective's 'what is it joined to and how' covers.

records.notes: Only the advanced tier was missing. Two numeric families were written, one per distinct skeleton, both with whole-number answers and no rounding. Checked by brute force over the parameter ranges: accel-values yields 320 distinct parameter sets, wavelength-values yields 145; every instance gives an integer answer. The misconception catalogue for this objective is empty, so no distractors or proposed misconceptions are used (neither family is mcq).

families.stem: Make $x$ the subject of the formula $y = {=a}px + {=b}qx$.
solution: $x$ is in both terms on the right-hand side, so take it out as a common factor: $y = x({=a}p + {=b}q)$.
$x$ is now multiplied by the bracket. Divide both sides by $({=a}p + {=b}q)$: $\frac{y}{{=a}p + {=b}q} = x$.
Write $x$ on the left: $x = \frac{y}{{=a}p + {=b}q}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill, modelled on book question ex4-5-9 (E = mgh + 1/2 mv^2, solve for m): the subject appears in exactly two terms, nothing else is on the subject's side, so the whole job is factorise then divide. Letters p, q, x, y are fixed; only the two coefficients a and b (2 to 9, different) change, giving 56 distinct stems. Coefficients are at least 2 so no '1px' is ever printed. Every instance's answer is x = y/(ap + bq); the denominator is never 0 because p and q are letters (the book's own note on restrictions, ex4-5-9, is not asked of the student here). No mcq, so no distractors and the catalogued misconception is not used.

params.why: the coefficient of ax after collecting must be at least 2, so no '1ax' is printed and x is not a whole number by accident
the answer is a fraction already in lowest terms, so 'simplest form' has one right answer

families.stem: Solve for $x$, given that $a \ne 0$: ${=p}ax + {=q}a - {=r}ax = {=s}ax - {=t}a$. Give $x$ as a fraction in simplest form.
solution: Move every term to the right-hand side, so that the left-hand side is $0$: $0 = {=s}ax + {=r}ax - {=p}ax - {=t}a - {=q}a$.
Collect like terms: $0 = {=den}ax - {=top}a$.
Both terms contain $a$, so take $a$ out as a common factor: $0 = a({=den}x - {=top})$.
The product is $0$ and $a \ne 0$, so the bracket must be $0$. (We may divide both sides by $a$ only because $a \ne 0$.) ${=den}x - {=top} = 0$.
Solve for $x$: ${=den}x = {=top}$, so $x = \frac{{=top}}{{=den}}$.
families.notes: Parametrised from book question ex4-7-12s (3ax + 2a - ax = 5ax - 6a). IMPORTANT BOOK ERROR: the book's printed answer and marker key is x = 3/8, but its own working reaches 3ax - 8a = 0, i.e. a(3x - 8) = 0, which gives x = 8/3. Substituting x = 8/3 into the stem confirms it (both sides equal 8a). This family computes the answer from the parameters (p=3, q=2, r=1, s=5, t=6 would give 8/3), so it is correct; the parent's key should be corrected or the reviewer should not trust it. Deliberate choice: the stem states a != 0, because the book prints no condition but its note says the solver may not divide by a unless a != 0; stating it makes the question unambiguous for a blind solver, and the solution step says explicitly why dividing by a is allowed (the catalogued misconception mc:g10m4s6-1-2:divide-by-unchecked-common-factor is therefore addressed in the working, not used as a distractor, because it does not change the final value and so cannot be a diagnosable wrong option). All coefficients are at least 2 so no '1ax' or '1a' appears (the book's own instance has a coefficient 1 and is not reproducible; that is intentional). den = s + r - p is in 2..12 and top = q + t is in 4..18, gcd 1, so the answer is always a non-integer fraction in lowest terms, checked by exhaustive sampling.

families.stem: Make $x$ the subject of the formula ${=a}x - py = {=b}x + qy$.
solution: Collect the terms containing $x$ on the left and the other terms on the right: ${=a}x - {=b}x = py + qy$.
Take out the common factor on each side: $x({=a} - {=b}) = y(p + q)$.
Simplify the bracket on the left: ${=k}x = y(p + q)$.
Divide both sides by ${=k}$: $x = \frac{y(p + q)}{{=k}}$.
families.notes: The subject x appears in a term on each side, so the student must first collect the x-terms on one side (the book's method in we16: isolate, collect, factorise, divide) and only then take x out as the common factor. Parameters: b in 2..8 and a = b + 2 .. b + 6, so a - b = k is always 2..6: never 0 (no division by zero), never 1 (no '1x'), never negative. The right-hand side p y + q y factorises to y(p + q), so both sides are factorised before dividing by the number k. Letters p, q, y are fixed; only a and b change (about 35 distinct stems). The answer (p + q)y/k is a single expression, so any equivalent arrangement is acceptable. No mcq, so no distractors.

families.stem: Make $x$ the subject of the formula $y = \frac{{=a}x}{x + {=b}k^{2}}$.
solution: Multiply both sides by the denominator $x + {=b}k^{2}$ to clear the fraction: $y(x + {=b}k^{2}) = {=a}x$.
Expand the bracket: $yx + {=b}yk^{2} = {=a}x$.
Get every term containing $x$ on one side: ${=b}yk^{2} = {=a}x - yx$.
Take out $x$ as a common factor: ${=b}yk^{2} = x({=a} - y)$.
Divide both sides by $({=a} - y)$: $x = \frac{{=b}yk^{2}}{{=a} - y}$.
families.notes: Same skeleton as book question we16 (h = R x H/(R + r^2), make R the subject): clear the fraction, expand, collect the subject's terms, take the subject out as a common factor, divide. The book's H and r^2 become the numeric coefficient a and the term b k^2, so only numbers change (a and b in 2..9, 64 distinct stems). The book's note about restrictions is not asked; the final expression is x = b y k^2/(a - y), which is equivalent to -b y k^2/(y - a), so either arrangement should be accepted. Verified by substitution for random values that the answer returns the original y. No mcq.

records.notes: Four families: one basic, two standard, one advanced. The two gaps (basic, standard) are filled. The standard slot has two families that are different skeletons: factor-a mirrors the book's only standard question ex4-7-12s, and bothsides is the formula version of the same method (collect the subject's terms, factor, divide). The advanced family reproduces the we16 skeleton as an extra, since the tier had no families. SLUG first-six check: twoter, factor, bothsi, fracti, all different. BOOK DEFECT FOUND: the key for ex4-7-12s (3ax + 2a - ax = 5ax - 6a) is printed as x = 3/8, but the book's own working gives a(3x - 8) = 0 and so x = 8/3; substituting confirms 8/3. The parent's marker key should be corrected, and the family factor-a is computed from its parameters so it is right. The one catalogued misconception (divide-by-unchecked-common-factor) is not used as a distractor, because no family is an mcq: the error does not change the final value, so no wrong option can be keyed to it. The factor-a stem states a != 0, and its working says why dividing by a is allowed. Param sampling and every algebraic identity were checked by exact rational substitution over thousands of random draws, since the engine itself was not available for a trial run (only the two packet files were opened, as instructed). Constructs used that the reviewer may wish to confirm the engine accepts: marker form {"subject": "x"} on kind equation with a one-letter subject on the left; kind expression with form "simplest" and a fraction template "{=top}/{=den}"; randint bounds as expressions ("b + 2", "b + 6"); LaTeX braces adjacent to holes as in \frac{{=a}x}{x + {=b}k^{2}}.

families.stem: Make $r$ the subject of the formula $V = {=a}r^2h$. Which one of the following gives every value of $r$ that satisfies the formula?
solution: Start with $V = {=a}r^2h$. Divide both sides by ${=a}h$ so that $r^2$ stands on its own: $r^2 = \dfrac{V}{{=a}h}$.
Take the square root of both sides. A square has a positive and a negative root, so write both signs: $r = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{V}{{=a}h}}$.
The root sign covers the whole fraction, so the answer is $r = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{V}{{=a}h}}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Stops at the squared variable
proposed_misconceptions.description: After dividing to isolate r squared, the student writes the quotient as if it were r and never takes the square root.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Roots only the numerator
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student takes the square root of the top of the fraction only and leaves the denominator outside the root sign.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Multiplies instead of dividing
proposed_misconceptions.description: To undo the coefficient multiplying the squared variable, the student multiplies both sides by it instead of dividing.

families.notes: Basic entry point, modelled on book Ex 4.5 Q5 (V = pi r^2 h) with the constant pi replaced by a whole number so the options stay plain. It is an mcq on purpose: the answer is a symbolic expression carrying a plus-or-minus sign, and every distractor is a named slip of this objective (positive root only, no root taken, root of the numerator only, multiply instead of divide). The stem carries the hole a, so instances differ by stem and distinct_by_choices is not needed. Options are not equivalent for any a from 2 to 15.

families.stem: Solve for $x$ in $V = x^2h$ if $V = {=vv}$ and $h = {=h}$. Give both values of $x$.
solution: Make $x$ the subject first. Divide both sides of $V = x^2h$ by $h$: $x^2 = \dfrac{V}{h}$.
Take the square root of both sides, writing both the positive and the negative root: $x = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{V}{h}}$.
Substitute $V = {=vv}$ and $h = {=h}$: $x = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{{=vv}}{{=h}}} = \pm\sqrt{{=x0*x0}} = \pm{=x0}$.
families.notes: Basic numeric partner to the mcq. Same one-squared-variable skeleton as Ex 4.5 Q5 and Q20: divide, take the root with both signs, substitute. V is built as x0 squared times h so the quotient is always a perfect square and both answers are whole numbers. The stem asks for both values, as the book key does for Q20 (h = 16 or h = -16).

families.stem: Solve for $a$ in $P = k\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ if $k = {=kk}$, $b = {=b0}$ and $P = {=pv}$. Give both values of $a$.
solution: Divide both sides of $P = k\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ by $k$ so the square root stands alone: $\dfrac{P}{k} = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
Square both sides to remove the square root: $\left(\dfrac{P}{k}\right)^2 = a^2 + b^2$.
Subtract $b^2$ from both sides: $a^2 = \left(\dfrac{P}{k}\right)^2 - b^2$.
Take the square root of both sides, writing both signs: $a = \pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{P}{k}\right)^2 - b^2}$.
Substitute $P = {=pv}$, $k = {=kk}$ and $b = {=b0}$: $a = \pm\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{{=pv}}{{=kk}}\right)^2 - {=b0}^2} = \pm\sqrt{{=h0}^2 - {=b0}^2} = \pm\sqrt{{=h0*h0 - b0*b0}} = \pm{=a0}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the unknown sits under a square root and the root has a coefficient, so the order is divide by k, square both sides, subtract b squared, then take the root with both signs. This is the book's c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) (Ex 4.5 Q11) with a coefficient added. Numbers come from five Pythagorean triples with the legs randomly swapped between a and b, so P / k = h is always whole and a is always a whole number. Triples checked: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 20-21-29. Largest P is 5 times 29 = 145.

params.why: so that E = m0 * v^2 / 2 is a whole number

families.stem: Solve for $m$ in $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E}{m}}$ if $v = {=v}$ and $E = {=en}$.
solution: Square both sides to remove the square root: $v^2 = \dfrac{2E}{m}$.
Multiply both sides by $m$: $v^2m = 2E$.
Divide both sides by $v^2$: $m = \dfrac{2E}{v^2}$.
Substitute $E = {=en}$ and $v = {=v}$: $m = \dfrac{2({=en})}{{=v}^2} = \dfrac{{=2*en}}{{=v*v}} = {=m0}$.
Here $m$ was never squared, so squaring both sides gives a single value and there is no plus-or-minus sign.
families.notes: Advanced twist: the variable under the root is in the denominator, so the method is square both sides (as in Ex 4.5 Q11) and then rearrange the fraction, and the answer is a single value because m is not the squared quantity. The numeric answer is the whole number m0. E is chosen as m0 * v^2 / 2 and instances with m0 * v^2 odd are rejected so E is always a whole number. Given v is positive, as a square root requires.

records.notes: Four families: two basic (one mcq on the symbolic plus-or-minus rearrangement, one numeric substitute-and-root) and two advanced (coefficient on a root with a sum of squares and a plus-or-minus answer; variable in the denominator under a root, squaring both sides with a single answer). The standard tier was not a listed gap (the book supplies five standard questions), so no standard family was written. Cube roots were left out because none of the book's questions for this objective use them. The symbolic plus-or-minus rearrangement is only offered as an mcq, because the plain marker syntax for a plus-or-minus symbolic key was not verifiable from the spec. All substitution families ask for both values, matching the book key for Ex 4.5 Q20 and Ex 4.7 Q8i.

families.stem: Solve for $\lambda$ in $t=\frac{D}{f\lambda}$ if $D={=D}$, $f={=f}$ and $t={=t}$.
solution: The variable $\lambda$ is in a denominator. In $t=\frac{D}{f\lambda}$ the only denominator is $f\lambda$, so it is the LCD.
Multiply both sides by the LCD, $f\lambda$: $t\times f\lambda=D$, that is $tf\lambda=D$.
Divide both sides by $tf$: $\lambda=\frac{D}{tf}$.
Substitute $D={=D}$, $f={=f}$ and $t={=t}$: $\lambda=\frac{{=D}}{{=t}\times{=f}}=\frac{{=D}}{{=t*f}}$.
So $\lambda={=L}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: one fraction, one denominator (f*lambda), numbers substituted at the end exactly as the book's ex4-5-21 and ex4-5-19 do. Built backwards from the answer L so D = t*f*L and lambda is always a whole number from 2 to 8. 112 distinct (f, t, L) triples. The book's ex4-5-8 asks for the symbolic form lambda = D/(tf); this is its numeric counterpart, which is why it is tagged basic.

families.stem: Solve for $u$ in $f'=f\frac{v}{v-u}$ if $v={=v}$, $f={=f}$ and $f'={=fp}$.
solution: The variable $u$ is in the denominator $v-u$, which is the only denominator, so it is the LCD. Multiply both sides of $f'=f\frac{v}{v-u}$ by $(v-u)$: $f'(v-u)=fv$.
Divide both sides by $f'$: $v-u=\frac{fv}{f'}$.
Subtract $v$ from both sides and multiply by $-1$: $u=v-\frac{fv}{f'}$.
Substitute $v={=v}$, $f={=f}$ and $f'={=fp}$: $u={=v}-\frac{{=f}\times{=v}}{{=fp}}$.
Simplify the fraction: $u={=v}-\frac{{=f*v}}{{=fp}}={=v}-{=g}$.
families.notes: Same skeleton as the book's ex4-5-19 (f' = f v/(v-u), solve for u), with the numbers built backwards so everything is a whole number: choose u, the gap g = v - u and a multiplier k, then v = u + g, f = k*g, f' = k*v. This makes f*v/f' exactly g, so the answer u = v - g is whole (the book's own numbers give 2.6; that case is deliberately not reproduced, to avoid a rounding instruction). Always f' > f and v > u, so no zero or negative denominators.

families.stem: Solve for $r_2$ in $\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{r_1}+\frac{1}{r_2}$ if $R={=R}$ and $r_1={=r1}$.
solution: The denominators are $R$, $r_1$ and $r_2$, so the LCD is $Rr_1r_2$. Multiply every term of $\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{r_1}+\frac{1}{r_2}$ by $Rr_1r_2$.
Each fraction cancels: $r_1r_2=Rr_2+Rr_1$.
Collect the terms containing $r_2$ on the left: $r_1r_2-Rr_2=Rr_1$.
Factorise out $r_2$: $r_2(r_1-R)=Rr_1$.
Divide both sides by $(r_1-R)$: $r_2=\frac{Rr_1}{r_1-R}$.
Substitute $R={=R}$ and $r_1={=r1}$: $r_2=\frac{{=R}\times{=r1}}{{=r1}-{=R}}$.
Simplify the numerator and the denominator: $r_2=\frac{{=R*r1}}{{=r1-R}}$.
families.notes: Same formula and same given/asked variables as the book's ex4-5-21 (1/R = 1/r1 + 1/r2, given R and r1, find r2). The book's instance r1 = 2, R = 3/2 is the case r2 = 6 here. R is built backwards as r1*r2/(r1+r2), so r2 is always a whole number; R is a fraction (or occasionally a whole number such as 2 for r1 = 3, r2 = 6). The solution follows the symbolic route (multiply by the LCD R*r1*r2, collect, factorise, divide) and substitutes at the end, like the book. r1 - R = r1^2/(r1+r2) is always positive, so no division by zero. 25 distinct (r1, r2) pairs.

params.why: a common factor of all three coefficients would let the answer be simplified, so the key would have more than one natural form

families.stem: Make $x$ the subject of the formula: $\frac{{=a}}{b}+\frac{{=c}b}{x}={=d}$.
solution: The denominators are $b$ and $x$, so the LCD is $bx$. Multiply every term by $bx$: $\frac{{=a}}{b}\cdot bx+\frac{{=c}b}{x}\cdot bx={=d}\cdot bx$, which simplifies to ${=a}x+{=c}b^{2}={=d}bx$.
Collect the terms containing $x$ on the left: ${=a}x-{=d}bx=-{=c}b^{2}$.
Factorise out $x$: $x({=a}-{=d}b)=-{=c}b^{2}$.
Divide both sides by ${=a}-{=d}b$: $x=\frac{-{=c}b^{2}}{{=a}-{=d}b}$, which can also be written $x=\frac{{=c}b^{2}}{{=d}b-{=a}}$.
Note restriction: ${=d}b\ne{=a}$, because the denominator cannot be $0$.
families.notes: Same skeleton as the book's ex4-5-4 (1/b + 2b/x = 2 gives x = -2b^2/(1-2b)), with the three numbers a/b + c*b/x = d varied. General result x = c*b^2/(d*b - a); the book's case is a = 1, c = 2, d = 2. a starts at 2 so that no instance prints a stray coefficient 1 (for example 1x). Whole-formula common factors are excluded by the gcd require, so the key is canonical; the equation marker should still accept the equivalent form x = -c*b^2/(a - d*b) that the book prints. Quick check: a=2, c=3, d=4, b=2 gives 1 + 6/x = 4, x = 2, and the formula gives 3*4/(8-2) = 2.

records.notes: Basic gap filled with one family; because no families existed yet, I also wrote the standard tier (two families with different skeletons: a binomial denominator, and a three-variable LCD) and one advanced family. The book's ex4-7-8h (S = a/(1-r)) was not given its own family because it has the same skeleton as the binomial-denominator family, and ex4-5-12 / ex4-7-8e (1/V = 1/U + 1/W type) would repeat the reciprocal-sum skeleton. No mcq families: there are no catalogued misconceptions for this objective, so no distractor could honestly name an error. Item-id prefixes are single, binomi, recipr and subjec, which are all different. I could not run the family engine in this session (only the two packet files could be opened), so the templates were checked by hand against the stated syntax and by working several instances through, not by executing them.

families.stem: Solve for $x$: $-{=a}x {=sym} {=c}$. Which one of the following is the solution?
solution: To get $x$ on its own, divide both sides of $-{=a}x {=sym} {=c}$ by $-{=a}$.
Dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign, so ${=sym}$ becomes ${=fsym}$.
$x {=fsym} \dfrac{{=c}}{-{=a}}$, which is $x {=fsym} {=s}$.
Check with $x = {=t}$: $-{=a} \cdot ({=t}) = {=pv}$, and ${=pv} {=sym} {=c}$ is true, so the solution is $x {=fsym} {=s}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Ignores the minus sign on the coefficient of x
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student reads $-ax$ as $ax$ and divides both sides by the positive number $a$, so the sign is not reversed and the boundary value comes out with the wrong sign (for example $-3x>12$ becomes $x>4$).

families.notes: Entry-point skill: one division by a negative coefficient, modelled on the book's own steps in ex4-6-2b (-3x <= 9 gives x >= -3), 2d and 2k, which divide by a negative number and reverse the sign. The inequality symbol is drawn as < or > (d), so the instances are not always answered with the same sign; coefficient a in 2..6 (a = 1 is left out so the stem never prints -1x), boundary s in -9..9 excluding 0 so the four options are always four different statements. The RHS is built backwards (c = -a*s) so the boundary is always a whole number and the working is exact. Options: correct x fsym s; keeps the sign (catalogued mc keeps-sign-after-negative); reads -ax as ax, giving x sym -s (new mc ignores-negative-coefficient); reverses the sign but divides the constant by +a, giving x fsym -s (no named error, null). Multiple choice is used because every wrong option is a specific sign error and the answer is an inequality; I did not use the plain interval marker for this family because I could not confirm how the marker syntax writes the infinite endpoint, and the book's interval-notation answers are all unbounded. Only the listed basic gap is filled. The book's standard exercises ask for interval notation, which needs that infinite-endpoint syntax confirmed, so no standard or advanced family was written.

records.notes: One family written for the listed basic gap. Standard and advanced were not authored because the book's standard exercises ask for interval notation (infinite endpoints) and the plain-marker syntax for infinity is not specified, and an mcq would not be an honest stand-in for those.
